note: Feedback for the Checks of Unit 9, read from the lesson files, where it was written with the lessons (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-27-chemstudy-unit-6-lessons-design.md). The option with no message is the answer. tests/e2e/check-feedback.spec.ts compares each lesson page with this file.

options.text: Helium leaving a pressurized cylinder to fill a party balloon
options.message: In the cylinder the helium atoms were squeezed into a small volume. Do they have more room in the balloon, or less?

options.text: Water vapor in a cloud condensing into raindrops
A puddle on a sidewalk drying up on a sunny afternoon
options.message: Drying is the liquid turning into vapor. Compare the room a water molecule has in the puddle with the room it has in the air.

options.text: Wax beside a candle's wick melting into a clear pool
options.message: Melting frees the wax molecules from their fixed places. Does that give them more ways to be arranged, or fewer?

options.text: Positive, because each molecule in the second drawing is larger
options.message: A larger molecule is still one particle. Count the separately moving particles in each drawing.

options.text: Zero, because the atoms, the volume and the temperature are unchanged
options.message: The atoms are the same, but are they grouped into the same number of separately moving particles?

options.text: Negative, because some of the atoms have left the sealed box
options.message: Count the atoms in each drawing: 8 × 2 and 4 × 4. The box is sealed.

options.text: Negative, because the same atoms now make up fewer gas particles
It is large and positive, because two new substances are formed
options.message: New substances form in every reaction. What sets the size of ΔS is the room the particles gain or lose. Count the moles of gas.

options.text: It is exactly zero, because 2 moles of gas become 2 moles of gas
options.message: The count is right: 2 moles of gas on each side. But are the four gases the same substance, with the same entropy for each mole?

options.text: It is small, and counting moles of gas cannot give its sign
Nothing can be said about its size or its sign without a table
options.message: Start with what you can count. How many moles of gas are on each side, and what does that say about the size of the change?

options.text: Equation A
options.message: This one makes 1 mole of gas from none. Find the change in the moles of gas for each of the other equations too.

options.text: Equation B
options.message: No gas appears on either side here, so the entropy changes little. Find the change in the moles of gas for each equation.

options.text: Equation C
options.message: It makes 10 moles of gas, but it starts with 9. What counts is the change in the moles of gas.

options.text: Equation D

options.message: The cylinder is rigid. Has the volume open to the atoms changed at all?

options.text: It stays the same, because neither the volume nor the amount changes
options.message: Volume and amount are the matter side of entropy. What does warming do to the energies of the atoms (topic 3.5)?

options.text: It falls, because the pressure of the gas goes up as it warms
options.message: The pressure rises because the atoms move faster. Ask how warming changes the way the energy is shared among the atoms.

options.text: A block of camphor left in a closet slowly shrinks until none is left
options.message: This change happens by itself, but which way does the entropy of the camphor go when a solid becomes a gas?

options.text: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas meet and form a white solid
Camphor vapor in a warm closet does not gather back into a solid block
options.message: This change would lower the entropy, and it does not happen. Does that argue against the claim, or agree with it?

options.text: A heap of rust on a shelf does not turn back into iron and oxygen gas
options.message: Rust turning into iron and oxygen would make a gas from a solid. Is that a fall in entropy? And does it happen?

options.text: At every temperature, because both terms of ΔG° are negative
Only above some temperature, where the entropy term outgrows ΔH°
options.message: That is the pattern when ΔH° is positive. This reaction releases energy, so which way does ΔH° point?

options.text: Only below some temperature, because heating works against it
options.message: Heating strengthens the entropy term. One mole of gas becomes three: does that term work for the reaction or against it?

options.text: At no temperature, because both terms of ΔG° are positive
options.message: Both terms positive would mean a reaction that takes in energy and loses entropy. Check each sign against the question.

options.text: ΔH° turns positive in a hot tube, so the reaction now takes in energy
options.message: This lesson takes ΔH° as the same at every temperature. Which term of the equation has T in it?

options.text: Molecules in a hot tube move too fast to react, so the smoke forms too slowly
options.message: Heating makes collisions more energetic and reactions faster. This is a question of which direction is favored, not of rate.

options.text: ΔS° is positive, and heating strengthens whichever way entropy points
options.message: Count the moles of gas on each side of the equation as written. What sign does that give ΔS°?

options.text: The entropy term works against the smoke, and at 700 K it outweighs ΔH°
Line 1, where ΔS° is put into kJ/K

options.text: Line 2, where the entropy term is found
Line 3, where the two terms are combined

options.text: Line 4, where the sign of ΔG° is read
options.message: A negative ΔG° does mean favored, so line 4 reads its number correctly. Find the first line where a number goes wrong.

options.text: The exact value of ΔG°, because a more negative ΔG° means a faster reaction
options.message: ΔG° compares the two ends of the reaction. Does anything in it describe the path between them?

options.text: The value of ΔH°, because a reaction that releases energy needs none to begin
options.message: ΔH° also compares only the two ends. Does the energy a reaction releases overall say anything about how it begins?

options.text: The activation energy, because the change needs that much energy to start
Nothing more, because years with no change show the mixture is at equilibrium
options.message: No change can mean two things. With ΔG° this negative, what would the jar hold if the reaction had gone as far as it can?

options.text: Gray tin is favored at 5 °C, but the change has a high activation energy
At 5 °C the two forms are at equilibrium, so neither one turns into the other
options.message: The two forms can sit in balance at one temperature only. What does the question say about ΔG° at 5 °C?

options.text: ΔG° must really be positive at 5 °C, or the bars would have crumbled by now
options.message: The question gives the sign of ΔG° at 5 °C as negative. A bar that has not changed does not overturn it.

options.text: The change must be endothermic, and a cold storeroom has too little energy to give
options.message: The energy a change takes in or gives out is already counted in ΔG°. What sign does the question give ΔG° at 5 °C?

options.text: It was at equilibrium, and the catalyst moved the equilibrium toward carbon dioxide
options.message: A catalyst speeds up the forward and the reverse reaction alike. Could it change a mixture in which the two already balance?

options.text: The change was unfavored there, and the catalyst made it favored
options.message: Hopcalite is not a reactant or a product. Can something outside the equation change which direction is favored?

options.text: It was far from equilibrium, and only a slow reaction kept it there
It was at equilibrium, and the hopcalite was used up changing the gas
options.message: A catalyst is still there, unchanged, at the end (topic 5.11). Which gas in the air supplied the extra oxygen atoms?

options.text: Mostly carbon monoxide and oxygen, since the catalyst can run the reaction either way
options.message: A catalyst does speed up both directions. Does speeding up both tell you which way a mixture moves?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, as good as unchanged, since $K$ is still about 10⁻⁹⁰
Carbon monoxide and oxygen, slowly, since a catalyst cannot speed up a reverse reaction
options.message: A catalyst speeds up the reverse reaction by the same factor as the forward one. What else, besides speed, decides what comes out?

options.text: It cannot be said until the activation energy on hopcalite is known
options.message: The activation energy sets how fast a change goes. Is speed the only thing that decides what comes out?

options.text: The share of collisions with enough energy to react
options.message: Warming a gas moves its collisions toward higher energies (topic 5.5). Would the share with enough energy to react stay where it was?

options.text: Breaking ATP's bond releases energy, and glutamate takes that energy in

options.text: ATP gives glutamate a phosphate group, so two reactions go as one

options.text: Carbon cuts the energy that must come from outside, but not to zero
The sum is above zero, so aluminum cannot be made from its oxide by any means
options.message: Read the last three words of this option again. How many ways of making an unfavored change happen has this lesson described?

options.text: A gas forms and the entropy rises, so the overall reaction must be favored
options.message: A rise in entropy is one term of ΔG°, and ΔG° already includes it. Add the two ΔG° values given.

options.text: A cell links amino acids into a protein, with ATP reacting at each step
options.message: ATP reacting is a favored chemical reaction. Is that a partner reaction, or a source of energy outside the chemistry?

options.text: Sodium takes the chlorine from TiCl₄ and leaves titanium metal
